lede: The new Prime Minister settles into Downing Street with a cabinet that marks a decisive break from the Starmer era, while the NHS reports early success in its meningitis vaccination catch-up campaign for university-bound students. Globally, markets opened the week buoyed by President Trump's decision to halt a planned strike on Iran ahead of Monday's resumption of talks, though the US-Iran conflict continues to keep energy prices elevated after six months of disruption to the Strait of Hormuz. On the regulatory front, the EU's AI Act transparency requirements came into force on Sunday, mandating disclosure when users interact with AI systems.
threeThings: Trump calls off planned Iran strikes, announcing US-Iran negotiations will resume Monday; oil briefly rose to $90 before easing on de-escalation hopes
The EU AI Act's transparency obligations became enforceable on 2 August, requiring AI systems to identify themselves to users and deepfakes to be labelled
NHS reports 89,261 first-dose meningitis B vaccinations in two weeks as its catch-up campaign targets students heading to university in September

items.headline: Burnham cabinet takes shape with Healey as Chancellor, Reeves out
items.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham completed his cabinet appointments on 23 July after taking office on 20 July. John Healey was appointed Chancellor in a surprise move, while Ed Miliband became Foreign Secretary and Shabana Mahmood remains Home Secretary. Rachel Reeves, David Lammy and Peter Kyle all left government. On his first day Burnham announced plans to scrap VAT on domestic electricity bills from 1 October.
items.why: The clearout of Starmer allies signals Burnham intends a genuine policy reset rather than continuity. The VAT move on energy bills is designed to demonstrate immediate cost-of-living relief while the new team develops its longer-term 10-year plan.

items.headline: Yvette Cooper appointed Health Secretary in cabinet reshuffle
items.summary: Yvette Cooper was appointed Secretary of State for Health and Social Care as part of Burnham's cabinet appointments on 21 July. Stephen Kinnock moved to become Secretary of State for Wales. Louise Haigh was appointed Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and will oversee a new Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
items.why: Cooper's move to Health suggests the new administration is prioritising NHS reform. Her background on home affairs may bring a different approach to the department's challenges around waiting lists and workforce planning.

items.headline: Bank of England holds rate at 3.75% as MPC split deepens
items.summary: The Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 on 30 July to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75%, with three members voting for a 0.25 percentage point increase to 4.00%. The Bank's central projection shows CPI inflation peaking at around 3.2% in Q4 2026. The MPC noted that risks to the inflation outlook are tilted to the upside amid the ongoing Middle East conflict's impact on energy prices.
items.why: The hawkish minority reflects genuine uncertainty about whether inflation will return to target given energy volatility. With no cuts priced in for 2026, the Bank is effectively on hold until clarity emerges on the geopolitical situation.

items.headline: NHS vaccinates 89,000 young people in MenB catch-up campaign
items.summary: Nearly 90,000 young people received their first dose of the meningitis B vaccine within two weeks of the NHS launching its catch-up campaign on 20 July. The NHS National Booking Service has received more than 135,000 bookings. The one-off programme targets all Year 13 pupils and those under 25 starting university for the first time in autumn 2026.
items.why: The programme responds to meningitis outbreaks earlier in 2026, including a cluster in Kent. Students heading to university halls are at elevated risk, and the timing ensures both doses can be administered before the autumn term when cases typically rise.

items.headline: UK house prices edge up 0.1% in July but annual growth slows
items.summary: UK house prices rose 0.1% month-on-month in July to an average of £277,542 according to Nationwide, the first gain in three months. However, annual growth slowed to 1.8% from 2.2% in June, a 20-month low. Mortgage rates have edged back up to around 4.75% in July as global uncertainty pushed up borrowing costs.
items.why: The market is caught between resilient demand and affordability pressures from higher rates linked to the Iran war's energy shock. The slowdown suggests buyers are becoming more cautious, though the absence of forced selling indicates no imminent crash.

items.headline: UK GDP growth forecast at 1% for 2026 as IMF downgrades outlook
items.summary: Independent forecasters surveyed by HM Treasury in July expect UK GDP growth of 1% in 2026, up slightly from 0.9% in June. The OBR's March forecast was for 1.1% growth. The OECD has noted the UK is particularly vulnerable to the global energy shock, with larger downgrades than other rich countries.
items.why: The UK's exposure stems less from energy imports than from inflation persistence and the knock-on effects on household spending and business confidence. The modest growth forecasts constrain fiscal space for the new government's reform agenda.

items.headline: Trump halts Iran strikes, announces Monday negotiations
items.summary: President Trump announced he had called off planned strikes on Iran over the weekend, citing requests from Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries and progress in talks. US-Iran negotiations are set to resume on Monday. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iran, and more than 50,000 American troops remain deployed in the Middle East as the conflict enters its sixth month.
items.why: Trump's pattern of threatened escalation followed by pullback makes it difficult to assess genuine progress versus tactical positioning. Any deal would likely require Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for sanctions relief, but neither side has shown willingness to move first.

items.headline: Hamas agrees to disarmament framework, but implementation uncertain
items.summary: Hamas and other Palestinian factions agreed on 30 July to a document setting out a plan for their disarmament in Gaza, brokered by Trump's Board of Peace. The demilitarisation process is expected to take 200-250 days. However, Israel has not officially agreed to the deal, and Hamas says it will not implement any part unless Israeli forces withdraw from Gaza.
items.why: The agreement creates a framework but not yet a functioning peace. Hamas's willingness to disarm is conditional on a Palestinian state, which Israel's government rejects. Israeli strikes continued the day after the announcement, underscoring the gap between declaration and implementation.

items.headline: Federal Reserve holds rates at 3.50-3.75% with three dissents
items.summary: The Federal Reserve kept its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.50-3.75% on 29 July, with Chair Kevin Warsh presiding over his first decision since taking office in May. Three FOMC members dissented, voting for a rate hike to combat above-target inflation. Warsh said the next major event would be his keynote at Jackson Hole from 27-29 August.
items.why: Warsh has emphasised changing how the Fed communicates, creating five task forces to examine monetary policy. The three dissents reflect concerns that inflation persistence from the Iran war may require tighter policy despite slowing growth.

items.headline: S&P 500 flat for July as tech volatility continues
items.summary: The S&P 500 closed at 7,489.72 on 31 July, up 0.7% on the day but down 0.1% for the month. The Nasdaq declined 3.2% in July while the Dow edged up 0.3%. Amazon jumped 15.3% on strong cloud growth, while Apple fell 7.3% after chip shortages raised costs. Markets are expected to open higher on Monday following Trump's Iran de-escalation.
items.why: August and September are historically weak months for equities, and 2026 is a midterm election year when volatility tends to be elevated. The Iran war has created inflationary pressure that now has markets pricing potential rate hikes rather than cuts.

items.headline: Brent crude at $87.93 after volatile July; monthly gain over 20%
items.summary: Brent crude finished July at $87.93 per barrel, up over 20% for the month as renewed hostilities between the US and Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has intensified as the temporary ceasefire collapsed, Yemen's Houthis expanded their attacks, and Saudi forces joined US operations. Oil briefly touched $100 in late July.
items.why: Five months of a mostly closed Strait of Hormuz have not sent prices to $150 as some feared, partly because demand has softened and alternative supply routes exist. But sustained closure or further escalation could still trigger the severe shock the World Bank warned of in April.

items.headline: EU AI Act transparency rules come into force
items.summary: On 2 August 2026, the EU AI Act's transparency requirements became enforceable. AI systems that interact with people must now disclose that the user is dealing with a machine. Deepfakes and AI-generated content must be labelled. Providers of generative AI models must mark outputs in a machine-readable way. The European Commission's AI Office begins enforcement alongside national authorities.
items.why: The deadline marks a significant but partial milestone. A late amendment pushed high-risk system requirements into 2027, so August 2026 primarily affects disclosure obligations rather than the full regulatory framework. Fines can reach €35 million or 7% of turnover.

items.headline: OpenAI's Astra model solves ten open mathematics problems
items.summary: OpenAI announced on 1 August that an internal version of its next major model, Astra, solved ten previously open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, publishing formal Lean proofs on GitHub. The problems include establishing the existence of non-sofic groups and new sphere-packing bounds. The compute cost was approximately $2,000.
items.why: This represents a qualitative shift from AI performing well on tests to contributing genuine discoveries in the most rigorous field. The verification via formal proofs distinguishes this from benchmark performance, but raises questions about how such capability will be governed.

items.headline: Three killed in Idaho In-N-Out shooting; gunman dead
items.summary: Three people were killed and seven injured when a gunman opened fire at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho on Saturday. The suspected shooter, 24-year-old Chad Williams, died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound after being confronted by an armed off-duty state trooper and a civilian. An In-N-Out employee was among the dead. The restaurant had opened just eight days earlier.
items.why: The incident is the latest in a series of US mass shootings and immediately reignited the gun control debate. The armed civilian response is being cited by both sides of the argument—as evidence that armed citizens save lives and that the prevalence of weapons creates the conditions for such attacks.

items.headline: Ukraine drones strike Russian oil refinery in Bashkortostan
items.summary: Ukrainian drones struck the Ufaneftekhim oil refinery in Bashkortostan on 1 August, according to Ukrainian military sources. Separately, drone attacks killed five people in Russia and set fire to a Wildberries warehouse. Russian forces launched 31 missiles, 66 air strikes with 201 guided bombs, and 6,659 kamikaze drones against Ukraine on the same day.
items.why: Ukraine continues to target Russian energy infrastructure as a way to impose economic costs while receiving diminished Western military aid. The deep strikes demonstrate retained capability but have not fundamentally altered the battlefield situation.

items.headline: US begins process of handing Ukraine military lead to Europe
items.summary: The US military has begun the process of transferring the lead role in Ukraine military assistance to European allies. The 2026 NDAA allocated $400 million for Ukraine through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative but the decision on spending lies with the administration. Parts of the Republican caucus in Congress oppose reducing support for Ukraine.
items.why: The shift reflects the Trump administration's strategy of using aid as leverage for negotiations while pressing European allies to bear more of the burden. Ukraine has estimated its 2026 defence needs at $120 billion, with half required from foreign partners.

items.headline: James Hansen warns 2026 likely to be warmest year on record
items.summary: Former NASA climate scientist James Hansen wrote in an update that 2026 is likely to be the planet's warmest year on record, despite starting cooler than 2024. He argues many scientists are still underestimating how sensitive Earth's climate system is to greenhouse gases. Climate Central has warned of summer heat spikes as global warming edges toward 2°C.
items.why: The forecast reflects both the underlying warming trend and the potential for short-term temperature spikes from changing ocean circulation patterns. The prediction adds urgency to COP 31 negotiations in Türkiye later this year.

items.headline: Trump administration targets 702 regulations for elimination
items.summary: The Trump administration's July 2026 Unified Agenda identified 702 existing rules for elimination, nearly double the number cut in Trump's first term. This is in addition to 752 regulatory cuts already finalised since October 2025. The EEOC has proposed rescinding EEO-1 reporting obligations, with review expected through mid-August.
items.why: The deregulatory push represents the administration's most aggressive effort to reshape the federal regulatory state. The scale of proposed cuts will face legal challenges and congressional scrutiny as the midterm elections approach.
